{{Short description|Study of smooth real-valued functions on manifold and their singularities}}
In [[mathematics]], at the junction of [[singularity theory]] and [[differential topology]], '''Cerf theory''' is the study of families of smooth real-valued functions

:<math>f\colon M \to \R</math>

on a [[smooth manifold]] <math>M</math>, their generic singularities and the topology of the subspaces these singularities define, as subspaces of the [[function space]]. The theory is named after [[Jean Cerf]], who initiated it in the late 1960s.

== An example ==

[[Marston Morse]] proved that, provided <math>M</math> is compact, any [[Smoothness|smooth function]] <math>f\colon M \to \R</math> can be approximated by a [[Morse theory|Morse function]]. Thus, for many purposes, one can replace arbitrary functions on <math>M</math> by Morse functions.

As a next step, one could ask, 'if you have a one-parameter family of functions which start and end at Morse functions, can you assume the whole family is Morse?'  In general, the answer is no.  Consider, for example, the one-parameter family of functions on <math>M=\mathbb R</math> given by

:<math>f_t(x)=(1/3)x^3-tx.</math>

At time <math>t=-1</math>, it has no critical points, but at time <math>t=1</math>, it is a Morse function with two critical points at <math>x=\pm 1</math>.

Cerf showed that a one-parameter family of functions between two Morse functions can be approximated by one that is Morse at all but finitely many degenerate times.  The degeneracies involve a birth/death transition of critical points, as in the above example when, at <math>t=0</math>, an index 0 and index 1 critical point are created as <math>t</math> increases.

== A ''stratification'' of an infinite-dimensional space ==

Returning to the general case where <math>M</math> is a compact manifold, let <math>\operatorname{Morse}(M)</math> denote the space of Morse functions on <math>M</math>, and <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)</math> the space of real-valued smooth functions on <math>M</math>. Morse proved that <math>\operatorname{Morse}(M) \subset \operatorname{Func}(M)</math> is an open and dense subset in the <math>C^\infty</math> topology.

For the purposes of intuition, here is an analogy. Think of the Morse functions as the top-dimensional open stratum in a [[Topologically stratified space|stratification]] of <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)</math> (we make no claim that such a stratification exists, but suppose one does). Notice that in stratified spaces, the [[co-dimension]] 0 open stratum is open and dense. For notational purposes, reverse the conventions for indexing the stratifications in a stratified space, and index the open strata not by their dimension, but by their co-dimension. This is convenient since <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)</math> is infinite-dimensional if <math>M</math> is not a [[finite set]]. By assumption, the open co-dimension 0 stratum of <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)</math> is <math>\operatorname{Morse}(M)</math>, i.e.: <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)^0=\operatorname{Morse}(M)</math>. In a stratified space <math>X</math>, frequently <math>X^0</math> is disconnected. The '''essential property''' of the co-dimension 1 stratum <math>X^1</math> is that any path in <math>X</math> which starts and ends in <math>X^0</math> can be approximated by a path that intersects <math>X^1</math> transversely in finitely many points, and does not intersect <math>X^i</math> for any <math>i>1</math>.

Thus Cerf theory is the study of the positive co-dimensional strata of <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)</math>, i.e.: <math>\operatorname{Func}(M)^i</math> for <math>i>0</math>. In the case of

:<math>f_t(x)=x^3-tx</math>,

only for <math>t=0</math> is the function not Morse, and

:<math>f_0(x)=x^3</math>

has a cubic [[degenerate critical point]] corresponding to the birth/death transition.

== A single time parameter, statement of theorem ==

The [[Morse theory#Morse lemma|Morse Theorem]] asserts that if <math>f \colon M \to \mathbb R</math> is a Morse function, then near a critical point <math>p</math> it is conjugate to a function <math>g \colon \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R</math> of the form

:<math>g(x_1,x_2,\dotsc,x_n) = f(p) + \epsilon_1 x_1^2 + \epsilon_2 x_2^2 + \dotsb + \epsilon_n x_n^2</math>

where <math>\epsilon_i \in \{\pm 1\}</math>.

Cerf's one-parameter theorem asserts the '''essential property''' of the co-dimension one stratum.

Precisely, if <math>f_t \colon M \to \mathbb R</math> is a one-parameter family of smooth functions on <math>M</math> with <math>t \in [0,1]</math>, and <math>f_0, f_1</math> Morse, then there exists a smooth one-parameter family <math>F_t \colon M \to \mathbb R</math> such that <math>F_0 = f_0, F_1 = f_1</math>, <math>F</math> is uniformly close to <math>f</math> in the <math>C^k</math>-topology on functions <math>M \times [0,1] \to \mathbb R</math>.  Moreover, <math>F_t</math> is Morse at all but finitely many times.  At a non-Morse time the function has only one degenerate critical point <math>p</math>, and near that point the family <math>F_t</math> is conjugate to the family

:<math>g_t(x_1,x_2,\dotsc,x_n) = f(p) + x_1^3+\epsilon_1 tx_1 + \epsilon_2 x_2^2 + \dotsb + \epsilon_n x_n^2</math>

where <math> \epsilon_i \in \{\pm 1\}, t \in [-1,1]</math>.  If <math>\epsilon_1 = -1</math> this is a one-parameter family of functions where two critical points are created (as <math>t</math> increases), and for <math>\epsilon_1 = 1</math> it is a one-parameter family of functions where two critical points are destroyed.

== Origins ==

The [[Piecewise linear manifold|PL]]-[[Schoenflies problem]] for <math>S^2 \subset \R^3</math> was solved by [[James Waddell Alexander II|J. W. Alexander]] in 1924. His proof was adapted to the [[Smooth manifold|smooth]] case by Morse and [[Emilio Baiada]].<ref>{{citation|last1=Morse|first1=Marston|authorlink1=Marston Morse| last2=Baiada|first2= Emilio|authorlink2=Emilio Baiada|title=Homotopy and homology related to the Schoenflies problem| 
journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=2|volume=58|year=1953|issue=1 |pages= 142–165|mr=0056922|doi=10.2307/1969825|jstor=1969825 }}</ref> The '''essential property''' was used by Cerf in order to prove that every orientation-preserving [[diffeomorphism]] of [[3-sphere|<math>S^3</math>]] is isotopic to the identity,<ref>{{citation|first=Jean|last=Cerf|authorlink=Jean Cerf|title= Sur les difféomorphismes de la sphère de dimension trois (<math>\Gamma_4=0</math>)|series= Lecture Notes in Mathematics|volume=53| publisher=Springer-Verlag|location= Berlin-New York|year= 1968}}</ref> seen as a one-parameter extension of the Schoenflies theorem for <math>S^2 \subset \R^3</math>. The corollary [[Exotic sphere|<math>\Gamma_4 = 0</math>]] at the time had wide implications in differential topology. The '''essential property''' was later used by Cerf to prove the [[Pseudoisotopy theorem|pseudo-isotopy theorem]]<ref>{{citation|first=Jean|last=Cerf|authorlink=Jean Cerf|title= La stratification naturelle des espaces de fonctions différentiables réelles et le théorème de la pseudo-isotopie|journal= [[Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS]] |volume=39 |year=1970|pages=5–173|doi=10.1007/BF02684687 }}</ref> for high-dimensional simply-connected manifolds.  The proof is a one-parameter extension of [[Stephen Smale]]'s proof of the [[h-cobordism|h-cobordism theorem]] (the rewriting of Smale's proof into the functional framework was done by Morse, and also by [[John Milnor]]<ref>[[John Milnor]], Lectures on the h-cobordism theorem, Notes by [[Laurent C. Siebenmann]] and Jonathan Sondow, Princeton Math. Notes 1965</ref> and by Cerf, André Gramain, and [[Bernard Morin]]<ref>[http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~aar/surgery/cerf-gramain.pdf Le theoreme du h-cobordisme (Smale)] Notes by Jean Cerf and André Gramain ([[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École Normale Supérieure]], 1968).</ref> following a suggestion of [[René Thom]]).

Cerf's proof is built on the work of Thom and [[John N. Mather|John Mather]].<ref>[[John N. Mather]],  Classification of stable germs by R-algebras, [[Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS]] (1969)</ref>  A useful modern summary of Thom and Mather's work from that period is the book of [[Marty Golubitsky]] and [[Victor Guillemin]].<ref>[[Marty Golubitsky]], [[Victor Guillemin]], Stable Mappings and Their Singularities. Springer-Verlag Graduate Texts in Mathematics 14 (1973)</ref>

== Applications ==

Beside the above-mentioned applications, [[Robion Kirby]] used Cerf Theory as a key step in justifying the [[Kirby calculus]].

== Generalization ==

A stratification of the complement of an infinite co-dimension subspace of the space of smooth maps <math>\{ f \colon M \to \R \}</math> was eventually developed by Francis Sergeraert.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Francis|last= Sergeraert |title=Un theoreme de fonctions implicites sur certains espaces de Fréchet et quelques applications|journal= [[Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure]] |series=(4) |volume=5 |year=1972|issue= 4 |pages= 599–660|doi= 10.24033/asens.1239 }}</ref>

During the seventies, the classification problem for pseudo-isotopies of non-simply connected manifolds was solved by [[Allen Hatcher]] and John Wagoner,<ref>[[Allen Hatcher]] and John Wagoner, Pseudo-isotopies of compact manifolds. Astérisque, No. 6. Société Mathématique de France, Paris, 1973. 275 pp.</ref> discovering [[K-theory|algebraic <math>K_i</math>]]-obstructions on <math>\pi_1 M</math> (<math>i=2</math>) and <math>\pi_2 M</math> (<math>i=1</math>) and by [[Kiyoshi Igusa]], discovering obstructions of a similar nature on <math>\pi_1 M</math> (<math>i=3</math>).<ref>Kiyoshi Igusa, Stability theorem for smooth pseudoisotopies. K-Theory 2 (1988), no. 1-2, vi+355.</ref>
